name: Felix Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior reporter on the online desk of the regional public broadcaster, mostly health and housing. A normal day starts with the 8:15 meeting, then I'm on the phone to the hospital press office, a tenants' group, or someone whose ceiling has mould on it. I file two or three web stories a day and sometimes cut a short piece for the radio bulletin. The best bit is when a story gets a landlord to actually fix something; the worst bit is waiting on hold.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's your contract like, and your life outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a fixed-term contract that runs to the end of 2027, which is normal for juniors there. I share a flat with two friends near the ring road, one's a teacher and one works in a call centre. I've got maybe a fortnight's money in the bank, because the rent ate the rest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I use the transcription tool for long interviews, because typing up an hour of a council housing officer is soul-destroying. I checked it against my notes the first few times and it was decent. I don't let it write anything, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent transcription tool and not much more, which is what I've been saying anyway. Online I'd probably share a thread about all the money companies wasted. At the pub I'd say, good, now fund the newsrooms instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly fine, because public money pays my wages, not ad clicks. The worry is the same as now: the contract ends in 2027 and they renew maybe half the juniors. AI being hype doesn't change the date on my contract, and the date on my contract is what keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing health and housing, keep using the transcription tool for the boring bit. I'd ask my editor, Rosa, in my next review what I need to do to be one of the juniors they keep. I'd stay in the union, because they're the ones who negotiated the renewal rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A bit of the usual worry about the contract, but that's life as a junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Rosa say last time you asked about renewal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She said bring her stories nobody else has. So I've been working on a long piece about damp in the council flats on Ash Road, which I do in my own time mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If they didn't renew you, where would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's only one other newsroom in this region and it's a commercial paper that pays less. I'd probably end up in a press office, which I'd find a bit sad, but I'd survive.

say: I'd say AI is a **decent transcription tool** and not much more.
I'd say at the pub that the money should go to **fund newsrooms** instead.
think: My wages come from **public money**, so the plateau barely touches me.
The real worry is my **contract ending** in 2027, with about half of juniors renewed.
do: Keep using **transcription** for long interviews and nothing more.
Ask **Rosa**, my editor, what earns a renewal at my next review.
Stay in the **union**, which negotiated the renewal rules.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with the usual worry about the **contract**.
S0.quote: AI being hype doesn't change the date on my contract, and the date on my contract is what keeps me awake.
fieldNote: Public funding makes him feel **sheltered** from the clicks economy.
His one real fear is a **fixed date**: the 2027 contract end.
He works on an **unpaid long piece** about damp flats to earn renewal.

steps.text: Keep using the transcription tool only for long interviews
Finish the Ash Road damp investigation to show Rosa at review
Stay a paying member of the broadcaster's union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should set the rules ourselves before management does, like which tasks the AI can touch and which it can't. Online I'd say public broadcasters have a duty to keep humans checking the news. I'd probably write a long post about it nobody reads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a lot of my day is rewriting press releases and summarising reports, and that's what the card says goes first. I think fewer juniors get renewed, maybe a third instead of half. I'm not top of the pile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly this time, not just transcription, so I'm the junior who knows how to check what the AI gets wrong. I'd push the union to get a written agreement on AI before 2027. And I'd start a small savings habit, fifty a month, before the contract question comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not hopeless. I'm good with people on the phone, and that's still mine for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would checking what the AI gets wrong actually look like in your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Say it summarises a hospital board report. I'd read the summary, then go to the bit about waiting times myself and ring the hospital to check. A summary can tell you the waiting list went down. A summary can't tell you it went down because they moved people to another list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the desk would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bilal, who does the overnight shift rewriting agency copy. That's basically the job the card describes. He's got a kid on the way.

say: I'd say staff should **set the rules** on which tasks AI can touch.
I'd say public broadcasters owe it to people to keep **humans checking** the news.
think: Much of my day is rewriting **press releases**, which goes first on the card.
Maybe only **a third** of juniors get renewed, and I'm not top of the **pile**.
do: Learn the AI tools properly so I'm the one who **checks the errors**.
Push the union for a **written AI agreement** before 2027.
Save **fifty a month** before the contract decision.
feel: **Anxious** but not hopeless; his **phone skills** feel like his for now.
S1.quote: A summary can tell you the waiting list went down. A summary can't tell you it went down because they moved people to another list.
fieldNote: He moves only once a change is **proven**, and this card proves it to him.
His pitch is to be the **error-checker**, a role he thinks humans keep.
He thinks of **Bilal** on the overnight desk before himself.

steps.text: Take the broadcaster's AI training beyond the transcription tool
Push the union for a written AI agreement before 2027
Set up a standing order saving fifty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs public money and a plan, now, not after. I'd be at whatever protest the unions called. Online I'd be saying the public broadcaster must keep human reporters because people need to trust what they hear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my contract wouldn't get renewed. If AGI can do any thinking work by 2028, then my contract ending in 2027 is basically the end. I'd be on the street just as it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start applying for anything with people in it straight away, maybe tenant advice at the housing charity I cover, because I know them. I'd ask my parents if I could move back to their place in the spring if it came to that. And I'd try to get the union to fight for redeployment, not just redundancy pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My contract ends in 2027 and the card says AGI comes in 2028, so I'd lose the job just as everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots for hands-on work come three years after the thinking AI. What does that change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the hands-on jobs last longer. My dad's a plumber, and he's always said I should've done a trade. In this one I'd seriously ask him about an apprenticeship, even at twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your flatmates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we might need to find a cheaper flat or a fourth person. The call-centre one, Jade, would be worse off than me, honestly.

say: I'd say this needs **public money** and a plan **now**.
I'd argue the broadcaster must keep **human reporters** for trust.
think: My **contract ends** in 2027, so it simply wouldn't be **renewed**.
I'd be out of work just as **AGI lands** in 2028.
do: Apply now for **tenant advice** work at the housing charity I cover.
Ask my dad about a **plumbing apprenticeship**, given robots come later.
Ask my parents if I can **move back** in the spring.
feel: **Alarmed**, with the contract date and the AGI date stacked together.
S2.quote: My contract ends in 2027 and the card says AGI comes in 2028, so I'd lose the job just as everyone else does.
fieldNote: He links the **contract date** and **AGI date** himself, which drives his alarm.
The **robot gap** turns his dad's old advice about a trade into a real option.
He thinks of **Jade**, his flatmate in a call centre, as worse off.

steps.text: Apply for tenant advice work at the housing charity
Ask his dad about starting a plumbing apprenticeship
Ask his parents about moving back home in the spring
Push the union to fight for redeployment over redundancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this decently: retraining money, a shorter working week, all of it. I'd be writing that in pieces and saying it at union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I probably get the contract renewed once, to 2029 or 2030, and then it's over. That's enough time to try one thing properly. Not enough to mess about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the renewal years to save hard, maybe a hundred a month, and to start a part-time course. Probably an evening course in housing law or advice, because it's what I already know from reporting. I'd keep using the AI tools at work, because being useful buys me the renewal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Five years feels like one more contract and then a door, so I'd want the next door picked before the first one shuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why housing advice rather than the plumbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm better at talking than at fixing pipes, if I'm honest. Housing advice still has a person in a room with someone who's scared, and I think people will want that even after 2031. Plumbing is the backup, because robots come later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep using the AI to buy the renewal. Isn't that helping the thing that replaces you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I know. I'd rather be the one in the room when it's set up than be left out of the room. It doesn't sit well, but I'd do it.

say: I'd say there's time for **retraining money** and a **shorter week**.
I'd make that case in **union meetings** and in my reporting.
think: I probably get **one more contract** and then the job is over.
Five years is enough to try **one thing properly**, not to drift.
do: Save **a hundred a month** through the renewal years.
Start an evening course in **housing law** and advice.
Keep using the **AI tools** at work to earn the renewal.
feel: **Anxious**, wanting the **next door** picked before this one shuts.
S3.quote: Five years feels like one more contract and then a door, so I'd want the next door picked before the first one shuts.
fieldNote: He sees **housing advice** as people work that outlasts the thinking AI.
He admits the **contradiction** of helping the tools that replace him.
Plumbing stays a **backup** because of the robot delay.

steps.text: Save a hundred a month during the renewed contract
Enrol in an evening course in housing law and advice
Use the newsroom's AI tools daily to earn the renewal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if governments use it, and a disaster if they waste it. I'd be pushing for the broadcaster to plan it openly with staff. I'd say it on the radio if they let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a career. I could be a proper reporter by then, maybe on the investigations team, and the thinking AI would hit me at thirty-seven. That's still young enough to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in journalism and get better at it, especially the bits that need people: finding sources, sitting in someone's kitchen. I'd learn the AI tools as they improve, without rushing. And I'd join the union's working group on AI, because I want a say in the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but more like the normal worry about a career. With ten years I'd get to be a real reporter first, which is all I wanted when I was nineteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in year eight or nine, when it's close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I'd want something lined up, probably housing advice or the charity sector. I'd have savings by then, hopefully, so I could take a pay cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd actually get my own place. I've not dared sign a long lease because of the contract, but with ten years I might.

I'd push the broadcaster to **plan openly** with its staff.
think: Ten years is **a career**; I could reach the **investigations team** first.
Thinking AI would hit me at **thirty-seven**, still young enough to change.
do: Get better at **people work**: sources, kitchens, knocking on doors.
Learn the AI tools **as they improve**, without rushing.
Join the union's **AI working group** to shape the plan.
feel: **Normal career worry**, with some **hope** of becoming a real reporter.
S4.quote: With ten years I'd get to be a real reporter first, which is all I wanted when I was nineteen.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **delay the pivot** and grow in journalism first.

steps.text: Pitch longer source-based stories to reach the investigations team
Join the union's working group on AI in the newsroom
Learn each new AI tool once colleagues have tested it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands right on top of my contract ending. What would help is redeployment rights in the union deal, and some kind of training grant so I could do housing advice or an apprenticeship without starving.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to trust. If every story sounds the same and nobody rings the tenant back, people will stop believing the news even when it's true. I think about that more than my own job, some days.

headlineQuote: If every story sounds the same and nobody rings the tenant back, people will stop believing the news even when it's true.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old** junior health and housing reporter at a regional **public broadcaster**.
He's on a **fixed-term contract** to 2027, shares a flat and has about a fortnight's savings.
He uses AI for **transcription only** and moves once something is proven.
His fear grows with the speed of AGI because it **collides with his contract** date.
His plans run through the **union**, housing advice work, and his dad's plumbing trade as backup.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it lands right as his contract **ends**.
whatWouldHelp: **Redeployment rights** in a union agreement on AI.
A **training grant** to cover housing advice study or an apprenticeship.
